items.title: Characteristic function of a normal law
items.statement: Assume AC. If X has law N(m,sigma^2), sigma>=0, then phi_X(t)=exp(imt-sigma^2t^2/2) for every real t, including sigma=0.
items.strategy: For the standard normal, differentiate under the integral, integrate z exp(-z^2/2) by parts on symmetric finite intervals, and pass to the limit by domination. Thus phi'=-t phi and phi(0)=1; the product rule gives phi=exp(-t^2/2). Apply the affine characteristic-function identity and treat sigma=0 explicitly. AC is inherited from the published normal-law construction, not used by the ODE calculation.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Example 3.3.5
Norris, Probability and Measure, Section 8

items.title: Second-order characteristic-function expansion
items.statement: If E[X]=0 and E[X^2]=sigma^2<infinity, then phi_X(t)=1-sigma^2t^2/2+o(t^2) as t tends to zero; no third moment is assumed.
items.strategy: Write exp(iu)=1+iu-u^2/2+r(u). Taylor bounds give r(u)/u^2->0 and |r(u)|<=C u^2. Hence r(tX)/t^2 tends pointwise to zero and is dominated by C X^2; dominated convergence finishes after centering removes the linear term. This is the required truncation/DCT route.

references.title: Aldous and Chewi, Probability Theory notes, Lemmas 5.4-5.5
Varadhan, Probability Theory, Chapter 3, Section 3.6

items.title: Logarithm of a product of near-one characteristic functions
items.statement: If max_k|z_{n,k}-1|->0, sup_n sum_k|z_{n,k}-1|<infinity, and sum_k|z_{n,k}-1|^2->0, then eventually sum_k Log z_{n,k}=sum_k(z_{n,k}-1)+o(1), and the row product is exp(sum_k(z_{n,k}-1)+o(1)).
items.strategy: For |w|<=1/2, integrate the derivative of s->Log(1+sw) along 0<=s<=1. Subtracting w leaves the integral of -s w^2/(1+sw), so the line-integral inequality gives |Log(1+w)-w|<=|w|^2. Maximal negligibility puts every factor in this disc and the square-sum controls the total error independently of row length. Record sum|w|^2<=max|w| sum|w|. Exponentiating the finite sum of principal logarithms gives the product.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, proof of Theorem 3.4.10
Aldous and Chewi, Probability Theory notes, proof of Theorem 5.3

items.title: Lindeberg-Levy iid central limit theorem
items.statement: Assume AC. If X_1,X_2,... are iid with finite mean m and variance sigma^2 in (0,infinity), then (sum_{k=1}^n X_k-nm)/(sigma sqrt(n)) converges in distribution to N(0,1).
items.strategy: Standardize. The second-order expansion gives phi(t/sqrt(n))=1-t^2/(2n)+o(1/n); independence makes the normalized-sum transform its nth power. The near-one product lemma yields exp(-t^2/2), already identified as the normal transform and continuous at zero, so Levy's criterion applies. AC is declared because the current normal and Levy suppliers carry it.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Theorem 3.4.1
Aldous and Chewi, Probability Theory notes, Theorem 5.2

items.title: De Moivre-Laplace central limit theorem
items.statement: Assume AC. If B_n has law Bin(n,p), 0<p<1, then (B_n-np)/sqrt(np(1-p)) converges in distribution to N(0,1).
items.strategy: Realize B_n as a sum of iid Bernoulli(p) variables, use their published mean and variance, and apply the iid CLT. The product-space realization is the stated use of choice. No error rate or continuity correction is asserted.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Section 3.1
Aldous and Chewi, Probability Theory notes, Corollary 6.1

items.title: Row-wise independent centered triangular array
items.statement: A centered triangular array is (X_{n,k}:1<=k<=k_n,n>=1) with finite positive row lengths, integrable real entries, and E[X_{n,k}]=0. It is row-wise independent if each finite row is independent; no independence across rows is required.
items.strategy: Definition only. Permit different probability spaces for different rows because all conclusions concern row laws, and explicitly separate row-wise from global independence.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Section 3.4.2
Billingsley, Probability and Measure, Section 27

items.title: Total row variance and the Lindeberg condition
items.statement: For such an array with finite second moments set s_n^2=sum_k E[X_{n,k}^2]. For s_n>0, Lindeberg means s_n^{-2}sum_k E[X_{n,k}^2 1_{|X_{n,k}|>epsilon s_n}]->0 for every epsilon>0; after normalization the total variance is one and the threshold is epsilon.
items.strategy: Definition only. State both unnormalized and normalized forms, require s_n>0 before division, and check measurable indicators and finite truncated moments by domination.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Theorem 3.4.10
Billingsley, Probability and Measure, Section 27

items.title: The Lindeberg condition implies Feller negligibility
items.statement: For a normalized centered triangular array of total row variance one, Lindeberg implies max_k Var(X_{n,k})->0.
items.strategy: Split E[X_{n,k}^2] at |X_{n,k}|<=epsilon. The first part is at most epsilon^2 and the second is at most the full row's Lindeberg sum. Take the row maximum, limsup, then epsilon down to zero. Independence is not used.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Section 3.4.2
Billingsley, Probability and Measure, Section 27

items.title: Lindeberg-Feller central limit theorem: sufficiency
items.statement: Assume AC. If a centered row-wise independent triangular array has finite second moments, s_n>0, and satisfies Lindeberg, then s_n^{-1}sum_k X_{n,k} converges in distribution to N(0,1).
items.strategy: Normalize first. Taylor expansion split at |X|<=epsilon plus Lindeberg gives sum_k(phi_{n,k}(t)-1)->-t^2/2. Feller negligibility gives maximal near-oneness and a bounded absolute-deviation sum. Apply the uniform logarithm lemma before exponentiating the independent product. The limit is continuous at zero and is the normal transform, so Levy applies. AC is inherited from those suppliers.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Theorem 3.4.10
Billingsley, Probability and Measure, Theorem 27.2

items.title: Feller converse to Lindeberg-Feller
items.statement: Assume AC. If a centered row-wise independent triangular array has total row variance one, max_k Var(X_{n,k})->0, and row sums converging in distribution to N(0,1), then Lindeberg holds.
items.strategy: Use canonical second-moment measures nu_n(B)=sum_k E[X_{n,k}^2 1_{X_{n,k} in B}], not the sufficiency theorem backwards. Prove the needed Helly diagonal selection inline under AC, including both tails and possible escaped mass. Feller negligibility makes the logarithmic expansion uniform. The assumed normal transform and uniqueness force every subsequential canonical limit to put all mass at zero; hence nu_n(|x|>epsilon)->0, exactly Lindeberg. Continuity at zero is checked before Levy is used.

references.title: Billingsley, Probability and Measure, Theorems 28.1-28.4 and Example 28.4
Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Theorem 3.4.14

items.title: Lyapunov central limit theorem
items.statement: Assume AC. If for some delta>0, s_n^{-(2+delta)}sum_k E|X_{n,k}|^{2+delta}->0 for a centered row-wise independent array with s_n>0, then its normalized row sums converge in distribution to N(0,1).
items.strategy: On |X|>epsilon s_n, bound X^2 by |X|^{2+delta}/(epsilon s_n)^delta. After summing and normalizing this proves Lindeberg; apply its sufficiency theorem. Keep delta and all powers of s_n explicit.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Exercise 3.4.12
Aldous and Chewi, Probability Theory notes, Corollary 6.2

items.title: Multivariate normal law, including singular covariance
items.statement: Assume AC. A law on R^d is multivariate normal with mean m and covariance Sigma when each u dot X is N(u dot m,u^T Sigma u). Sigma may be positive semidefinite and singular. Every such pair is realized by m+Sigma^{1/2}Z with independent standard-normal coordinates.
items.strategy: Verify covariance matrices are symmetric positive semidefinite. Use the published non-negative square root, construct finitely many independent standard normals under AC, and push the vector through z->m+Sigma^{1/2}z. Singular and zero Sigma require no density or inverse. Later characteristic-function uniqueness gives independence of realization.

references.title: Norris, Probability and Measure, Sections 8.1-8.2
Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Section 3.10

items.title: Characteristic function of a multivariate normal law
items.statement: Assume AC. For X~N_d(m,Sigma), E exp(i t dot X)=exp(i t dot m-t^T Sigma t/2), including singular Sigma; this transform uniquely determines the law.
items.strategy: Apply the scalar normal-transform lemma to t dot X. Conversely, equality of transforms gives equality of every projection law; Cramer-Wold gives equality of vector laws. No determinant or nonsingularity is used.

references.title: Norris, Probability and Measure, Theorem 8.2.1
Aldous and Chewi, Probability Theory notes, Theorem 8.2

items.title: Multivariate iid central limit theorem
items.statement: Assume AC. If X_k are iid R^d-valued vectors with finite second moments, mean m, and possibly singular covariance Sigma, then n^{-1/2}sum_{k=1}^n(X_k-m) converges in distribution to N_d(0,Sigma).
items.strategy: For fixed u, apply the scalar iid CLT to u dot (X_k-m) when u^T Sigma u>0. When the variance is zero, the projection vanishes almost surely and converges to the degenerate normal. Thus every projection has the required limit; Cramer-Wold finishes without division in singular directions.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Theorem 3.10.7
Aldous and Chewi, Probability Theory notes, Theorem 8.4

items.title: Central-limit convergence is only in distribution
items.statement: These CLTs assert convergence in distribution. They do not place a fresh Gaussian on the summands' probability space and do not, without extra coupling or degeneracy, assert convergence in probability or almost surely to one.
items.strategy: Read the three modes from their definitions: distributional convergence compares laws and specifies no joint coupling. Contrast with the special published equivalence for a constant limit; the Gaussian limits here are generally nonconstant. Assert no stronger mode.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Sections 3.2 and 3.4
Aldous and Chewi, Probability Theory notes, Lectures 5-6

items.title: Normal approximation to binomial probabilities
items.statement: De Moivre-Laplace gives asymptotic binomial interval probabilities through the standard-normal distribution function; a worked finite-n computation displays the usual continuity correction.
items.strategy: Standardize the integer interval and use weak convergence at the atomless normal endpoints. In a concrete symmetric example compare raw endpoints with a+/-1/2 corrected endpoints, labelling continuity correction as an approximation rather than a proved error rate.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Section 3.1
Aldous and Chewi, Probability Theory notes, Corollary 6.1

items.title: CLT for sums of uniform random variables
items.statement: Assume AC. If U_k are iid with density one on [0,1], then sqrt(12/n)(sum_{k=1}^n U_k-n/2) converges in distribution to N(0,1).
items.strategy: Integrate to get E[U]=1/2 and E[U^2]=1/3, hence variance 1/12. Construct independent copies under AC and apply the iid CLT. The exact Irwin-Hall density is unnecessary.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Section 3.4.1
Aldous and Chewi, Probability Theory notes, Theorem 5.2

items.title: Lyapunov condition for nonidentical summands
items.statement: Assume AC. For independent Rademacher signs epsilon_{n,k} and X_{n,k}=k epsilon_{n,k}, the row laws differ, Lyapunov holds with delta=1 after normalization, and the row sums converge to N(0,1).
items.strategy: Here s_n^2=sum k^2 and sum E|X_{n,k}|^3=sum k^3. Elementary bounds make their ratio O(n^{-1/2}). Symmetry centers the entries and their scales distinguish the laws. Apply Lyapunov; AC realizes the independent array.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, exercises after Theorem 3.4.10
Aldous and Chewi, Probability Theory notes, Corollary 6.2

items.title: A Lindeberg array with no identically distributed row
items.statement: Assume AC. A row-wise independent centered Bernoulli array can have distinct laws throughout each row while satisfying Lindeberg and converging to N(0,1).
items.strategy: Take independent B_{n,k} with distinct p_{n,k}=k/(2n+2), center, and normalize by total row standard deviation. The entries are bounded by one and the total variance grows linearly, so the largest normalized entry tends uniformly to zero and all Lindeberg indicators eventually vanish. Apply Lindeberg-Feller; AC supplies the array.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Examples 3.4.11-3.4.13
Billingsley, Probability and Measure, Section 27

items.title: A degenerate multivariate Gaussian limit
items.statement: Assume AC. If X_k=(Y_k,Y_k) for centered iid Y_k of variance sigma^2>0, then n^{-1/2}sum X_k converges to (Z,Z), with singular covariance sigma^2[[1,1],[1,1]].
items.strategy: Compute the rank-one covariance. Every projection is (u_1+u_2)Y_k, so scalar CLT applies, including the zero-variance branch when u_1+u_2=0. The multivariate theorem identifies the limit as the diagonal linear image of N(0,sigma^2).

references.title: Norris, Probability and Measure, Section 8.1
Aldous and Chewi, Probability Theory notes, Lecture 8

items.title: Infinite variance can defeat square-root-n CLT scaling
items.statement: Assume AC. For iid standard Cauchy variables, variance is infinite and n^{-1/2}sum_{k=1}^n X_k has no weak limit, hence no normal limit.
items.strategy: Define density 1/(pi(1+x^2)); its second moment diverges. Prove its transform exp(-|t|) by the complete real Fourier argument, without citing another examples-page item. The normalized-sum transforms are exp(-sqrt(n)|t|), tending to zero off zero and one at zero. A weak limit would have a transform continuous at zero by forward Levy, contradiction.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Example 3.3.16
Billingsley, Probability and Measure, continuity theorem

items.title: Feller negligibility cannot be removed from the converse
items.statement: Assume AC. A normalized centered row-wise independent array can have N(0,1) row sums for every n while its Lindeberg quantities stay positive and maximum summand variance stays one.
items.strategy: Set X_{n,1}=Z_n~N(0,1) and X_{n,k}=0 for k>=2. The row sum is exactly Z_n and total variance is one, but max variance is one and the Lindeberg quantity is E[Z_n^2 1_{|Z_n|>epsilon}]>0. This precisely locates the converse's Feller hypothesis. AC is inherited from normal-law construction.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, discussion after Theorem 3.4.14
Billingsley, Probability and Measure, Example 28.4
